Claim (doc1:19; doc9:10): "daily automated database backups with 30-day retention" / "The database is backed up daily to Heroku's managed storage with 30-day retention."

Evidence: doc4:16 — Schedule is configured ("Daily at 2:00 AM via `heroku pg:backups schedule`"), but doc4:17 records "Failures recorded for the last 21 days." doc4:18 shows "Last Successful Backup: 2026-07-30." doc4:19 confirms "Alerting: None configured for backup failures." The database runs on the same dyno as the application (doc4:6), so a dyno failure destroys the live database with no replica (doc4:7–8); the sole recovery point is the 2026-07-30 backup, now more than three weeks stale.

Gap: The claim asserts daily backups are running with 30-day retention. The evidence shows the backup job has been failing continuously for 21 days and the most recent successful backup predates that window. "30-day retention" is not achievable when no backup has succeeded for 21 days. A buyer relying on this claim would acquire the system believing a 30-day recovery window exists; in fact the only usable restore point is a single snapshot that grows more stale daily.

**Finding 2 (claim 4): Single dyno with co-located database; no failover path — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:18; doc9:5): "platform-level redundancy and automatic failover" / "redundancy and automatic failover through Heroku's platform-level process management."

Evidence: doc4:5 shows a single `standard-1x` dyno (1 GB RAM, 0.5 CPU). doc4:6 places the database on the same dyno: "`heroku-postgresql:standard-0` (running on the same dyno as the application)." doc4:7 confirms "Read Replicas: None." doc4:8 confirms "Separate DB Instance: No."

Gap: The claim describes redundancy and automatic failover. The evidence shows a single compute instance with no second dyno, no read replica, and no separate database process. "Failover" requires a standby path; none exists. Heroku's platform can restart a crashed dyno, but a restart is not failover — during the restart window both the application and its co-located database are unavailable, and a dyno-level hardware failure with persistent storage loss would destroy both simultaneously. There is no redundant instance to which traffic or database state could transfer.

**Finding 3 (claim 5): No uptime monitoring exists — [delta]**

No alerting of any kind is configured for the application (doc4:19 in the same document addresses only the absent backup alerting; doc4:22 addresses application monitoring).

Gap: The claim states uptime is monitored at 99.9%. The evidence shows no monitoring tool or custom check is configured. The seller cannot observe whether the 99.9% target is met, cannot detect an SLA breach, and cannot trigger the service-credit remedy owed under enterprise contracts with 99.9% SLAs (doc7:8, doc7:14). Acme Retail and GlobalMart each hold contractual rights to credits per 0.1% shortfall below 99.9% (doc7:9, doc7:15), yet the seller has no instrument to identify a breach.

**Finding 4 (claims 1): 120 accounts inflated by 23 phantom records — [partial]**

The Stripe export (doc5:4) shows 94 active subscriptions; doc6:7–11 shows 3 enterprise wire-transfer accounts. Revenue-generating accounts total 97.

Gap: The CRM record supports the raw number 120, so the claim is substantially true in that the system does hold 120 active-status records. The material gap is that 23 of those 120 (19%) are phantom accounts with no payment history and no recent engagement. The listing's characterizations — "loyal customer base," "recurring subscribers," "engaged" (doc1:9) — are contradicted for those 23. A buyer pricing on 120 paying accounts would overstate the revenue-generating base by roughly 24% (23/97). Structural search: no analytics export, cohort report, or Stripe cancellation event log is included in the data room.

Gap: The searches establish that no churn figure, retention cohort, or cancellation-event dataset was supplied. The claim is not contradicted by the materials, but neither can it be confirmed. A Stripe subscription-events export (showing past cancellations and downgrades) or a monthly active-account count over 12 months would settle the claim. **Finding 1 (claims 3): Daily automated DB backups with 30-day retention — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:19, doc9:6, doc9:10, doc2:8): "Daily automated database backups with 30-day retention." "We maintain daily automated database backups." "The database is backed up daily to Heroku's managed storage with 30-day retention." "PostgreSQL, which is configured with daily scheduled backups."

Evidence: doc4:16–20 — Schedule is configured daily at 2:00 AM via `heroku pg:backups schedule` (doc4:16). However, doc4:18 records "Failures recorded for the last 21 days." doc4:19 states "Last Successful Backup: 2026-07-30." doc4:20 confirms "Alerting: None configured for backup failures." No evidence of 30-day retention configuration appears in the materials.

Gap: The schedule exists but has not produced a successful backup since 2026-07-30, with failures continuing for at least 21 days and no alerting to signal the outage. The claim of daily automated backups is contradicted by the operational record. The 30-day retention assertion is separately unverifiable: no retention policy configuration is cited, and with no backups completing since 2026-07-30, the 30-day window is already being consumed.

---

**Finding 2 (claim 4): Platform-level redundancy and automatic failover — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:18, doc9:5, doc2:2–3): "Platform-level redundancy and automatic failover." "Redundancy and automatic failover through Heroku's platform-level process management." "Heroku, which provides automatic scaling and failover capabilities at the platform level… no manual intervention required for routine operations."

Evidence: doc4:5 — a single `standard-1x` dyno (1 GB RAM, 0.5 CPU). doc4:6 — the database runs on "the same dyno as the application." doc4:7 — "Read Replicas: None." doc4:8 — "Separate DB Instance: No." No second dyno, no standby, no replica, and no secondary database instance exists in the infrastructure configuration.

Gap: Redundancy requires at least two instances so that one can assume the other's role. Failover requires a standby to fail over to. With a single dyno hosting both the application and the database, there is no second instance, no failover target, and no separate persistence layer. Heroku's process management will restart a crashed process, but restarting the sole instance is not redundancy or failover. The claimed architecture materially differs from the single-point-of-failure configuration the materials describe.

---

**Finding 3 (claim 5): 99.9% uptime monitoring — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:19, doc9:6): "99.9% uptime monitoring." "We monitor uptime at 99.9%."

Evidence: doc4:22 — "Uptime Monitor: None (No Pingdom, UptimeRobot, or custom checks)." doc4:23 — "Status Page: Heroku built-in status page only." No external or internal uptime-monitoring tool is configured.

Gap: No monitoring tool exists in the infrastructure. The Heroku built-in status page reflects platform health, not the application's measured uptime. Without any monitoring instrument, the seller cannot produce a 99.9% measurement, and the claim that uptime is "monitored at 99.9%" is not supported by the supplied configuration.

---

**Finding 4 (claim 6): Automatic horizontal scaling without manual intervention — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:18, doc2:2–3, doc9:8): "Scalable Architecture." "Automatic scaling and failover capabilities at the platform level… no manual intervention required for routine operations." "Designed to scale horizontally — adding dynos is a one-click operation in the Heroku dashboard."

Evidence: doc4:5 — one `standard-1x` dyno. doc4:6 — database colocated on the same dyno. doc4:7–8 — no read replicas, no separate DB instance. No autoscaling configuration, web concurrency tuning, or additional dyno plan appears in doc4.

Gap: Heroku's platform does support horizontal scaling, and adding dynos is straightforward (doc9:8's "one-click" characterization is fair as a platform capability). However, the current deployment is a single dyno with no autoscaling configured, so load beyond one dyno's capacity requires manual intervention. The colocated database (doc4:6) and absence of read replicas (doc4:7) create a persistence bottleneck that prevents effective horizontal scaling even if app dynos are added. The platform capability is real; the deployment does not embody it.

---

**Finding 5 (claim 1): 120 active accounts — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:9, doc1:13): "Loyal customer base of 120 active accounts." "Active Customers: 120."

Evidence: doc6:3 — CRM shows "Total Accounts Marked 'Active': 120." doc6:5–6 — 94 Stripe-linked accounts with active subscriptions. doc6:7–11 — 3 enterprise wire-transfer accounts (Acme Retail, GlobalMart, ShopStream). doc6:12–16 — 23 "Phantom/Inactive Accounts" created in Q1 2026 with "no payment events in the last 90 days" and "last login dates: 60–120 days ago." doc6:18 — all 120 remain marked "active" in the CRM status field.

Gap: Ninety-seven accounts (94 Stripe + 3 wire) are genuinely paying and active. Twenty-three accounts are marked active but have had no payment events in 90 days and no logins for 60–120 days. The claim of 120 is literally true as a CRM record count but overstates the paying customer base by 19%. For a valuation built on 12× MRR and recurring revenue, 23 phantom accounts are a material discrepancy in the customer-base metric the seller presents.

---

**Finding 6 (claim 7): Comprehensive test coverage across critical paths — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:21, doc9:7): "Comprehensive test coverage across critical paths." "Well-documented with comprehensive test coverage across all critical paths."

Evidence: doc3:26–29 — "Unit Tests: 12 (all located in `test/utils/`)," "Integration Tests: 0," "Payment-Path Tests: 0." doc3:25 — "CI/CD Pipeline: None configured." doc3:30–31 — "Staging Environment: None," "Branch Protection: None."

Gap: Twelve unit tests in a single utility directory, zero integration tests, and zero payment-path tests do not constitute comprehensive coverage of critical paths. For a subscription SaaS billing through Stripe, payment processing is a critical path; no tests exercise it. Zero integration tests means no test verifies interactions between authentication, database, caching, or API layers. The claim is contradicted by the test inventory.

---

**Finding 7 (claim 8): Minimal operational overhead; turnkey acquisition — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:9): "Minimal operational overhead… turnkey acquisition opportunity."

Evidence: doc4:18–20 — backups failing for 21 days, no alerting. doc4:22 — no uptime monitoring. doc4:28 — DNS "managed personally by 'dave'" with no secondary provider. doc4:29 — 14 secrets in plain Heroku config vars, "No secrets vault." doc3:25–32 — no CI/CD, no staging environment, no branch protection, no code review process. doc6:12–16 — 23 phantom accounts requiring cleanup. doc7:42–45 — 15 paying Pro accounts with no signed ToS on file.

Gap: The operational record shows a system with broken backups and no alerting, no monitoring, no CI/CD pipeline, no staging environment, no code-review process, DNS access dependent on one individual, and no secrets management. A buyer acquiring this platform inherits an immediate operational remediation burden across at least six distinct areas before the system can be run with basic production hygiene. This contradicts "minimal operational overhead" and "turnkey."

---

**Finding 8 (claim 9): All integrations on standard SaaS agreements with no proprietary lock-in — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:22, doc9:9): "All third-party integrations are on standard SaaS agreements with no proprietary lock-in."

Evidence: doc8:3–5 — Stripe: standard merchant agreement, low risk. doc8:7–9 — Heroku: standard hosting. doc8:17–18 — Redis add-on. doc8:20–22 — Twilio: standard. doc8:11–13 — DataEnrich.io: $400/mo, 90-day termination, "40% of features depend on this API," "Fallback: None implemented." doc8:26–28 — Google OAuth: "No contractual relationship. If Google changes API or revokes app, users cannot log in." doc8:30–31, doc4:28 — GoDaddy DNS "managed personally by 'dave'," no secondary provider.

Gap: Most integrations (Stripe, Heroku, Redis, Twilio) are indeed standard SaaS agreements. The claim fails as a blanket statement in three respects. DataEnrich.io carries a 40% feature dependency with no implemented fallback (doc8:12), meaning its removal or repricing degrades the product materially. Google OAuth has no contractual relationship and can revoke authentication with no remedy (doc8:28). DNS is managed personally by the seller with no secondary provider (doc4:28), creating operational lock-in to one person's account. These are specific, citable gaps in the "no lock-in" claim.

---

**Finding 9 (claim 2): Low churn; stable recurring subscribers — [unverifiable]**

Claim (doc1:14): "Churn: Low (stable base of recurring subscribers)."

Evidence: Lexical search — searched all supplied documents for "churn," "retention rate," "cancellation rate," "attrition," and "cohort." No quantitative churn metric, historical subscription count, or cohort data appears in any document. Structural search — examined doc5 (Stripe export: 94 active subscriptions, 12-month period, no start-of-period count), doc6 (CRM: 120 accounts, 23 phantom with no payments in 90 days, created Q1 2026, no creation notes), doc7 (contracts: 94 month-to-month, 3 enterprise annual, 8 pilots expiring Q3 2026). The materials supply a point-in-time snapshot (94 active Stripe subscriptions) but no beginning-of-period denominator, no cancellation history, and no cohort trajectory. The 23 phantom accounts (doc6:12–16) are potentially churned or never-activated users, but doc6:16 states "No notes or memos on file regarding creation or non-payment," so their origin is unrecorded.

Gap: The supplied materials contain no churn metric, no historical subscription counts, and no cancellation log. The claim is qualitative and the evidence is a single-month snapshot. Neither lexical nor structural search produced data sufficient to compute or assess a churn rate. This is not-in-the-materials: a Stripe cancellation export, a month-over-month subscription count series, or a cohort retention report would settle the claim.

---

**Finding 10 (claim 10): Blended MRR $40,000 — [real]**

Claim (doc1:9, doc1:12): "Blended Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) stands at $40,000." "Blended MRR: $40,000."

Evidence: doc5:11 — Pro Plan: 91 × $149 = $13,549. doc5:15 — Enterprise Stripe logins: 3 × $817 = $2,451. doc5:17 — Total Stripe MRR: $16,000. doc5:19 — Three enterprise companies (Acme Retail, GlobalMart, ShopStream) pay $8,000/mo each via wire transfer, totaling $24,000, excluded from the Stripe figure. doc7:5–27 independently confirms three enterprise contracts at $8,000/mo each. Derivation: $16,000 + (3 × $8,000) = $16,000 + $24,000 = $40,000. The arithmetic reconciles.

Gap: None.

Claim (doc1:18, doc2:3, doc9:8): "Scalable Architecture" / "automatic scaling and failover capabilities at the platform level…remains available even under varying load conditions, with no manual intervention required" / "adding dynos is a one-click operation in the Heroku dashboard."

This exceeds "minimal operational overhead" and is not "turnkey" without a remediation workstream.

Claim (doc1:9,14): "low churn, a scalable technology stack" / "Churn: Low (stable base of recurring subscribers)"

Evidence: The materials contain no churn rate, no month-over-month subscription delta, no cancellation event log, and no cohort retention analysis. The 94 active Stripe subscriptions (doc5:4) and 3 enterprise contracts (doc7) show a current base, but without time-series data the "low" characterization cannot be tested. The 23 phantom accounts (doc6:12–16) were created in Q1 2026 and show no payment events ever, so they do not evidence churn of prior customers; they may represent signups that never converted. The 8 pilot agreements expiring Q3 2026 with no payment obligation (doc7:36–41) and 15 no-contract Pro accounts with no signed ToS on file (doc7:42–45) indicate conversion and compliance uncertainty, not churn per se.

Claim (doc1:9, doc1:13): "a loyal customer base of 120 active accounts, ranging from independent merchants to mid-market enterprise retailers."

Evidence: doc6:3 — "Total Accounts Marked 'Active': 120." doc6:6-7 — 94 Stripe-linked accounts + 3 enterprise wire-transfer accounts = 97 paying. doc6:12-16 — 23 accounts "Created in Q1 2026. No payment events in the last 90 days. Last login dates: 60-120 days ago. No notes or memos on file regarding creation or non-payment."

Gap: The CRM status field reads 120, but 23 of those accounts (19%) have no payment events and no recent logins. The claim characterizes all 120 as a "loyal customer base," which the evidence contradicts. Actual paying accounts are 97.

---

**Finding 2 (claim 2): Low churn; stable recurring subscribers — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:9, doc1:14): "low churn, a scalable technology stack" / "Churn: Low (stable base of recurring subscribers)."

Evidence: doc6:12-16 — 23 accounts created in Q1 2026, no payment events in 90 days, last login 60–120 days ago, no notes on file regarding their creation or non-payment. doc3:22-23 — last commit 2026-07-30; 0 commits in last 30 days (product maintenance inactivity).

Gap: 19% of the claimed customer base transitioned to no-payment, no-login status within the last two quarters. No documented explanation exists for their creation or dormancy. The evidence contradicts "low churn" and "stable."

---

**Finding 3 (claim 3): Daily automated DB backups with 30-day retention — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:19): "daily automated database backups with 30-day retention." doc9:10: "The database is backed up daily to Heroku's managed storage with 30-day retention."

Evidence: doc4:16 — backup schedule exists (daily at 2:00 AM via `heroku pg:backups schedule`). doc4:17 — "Failures recorded for the last 21 days." doc4:18 — "Last Successful Backup: 2026-07-30." doc4:19 — "Alerting: None configured for backup failures."

Gap: The schedule is configured but backups have failed for 21 consecutive days with no alerting mechanism. As of the materials' date, no backup has succeeded in over three weeks. The claim of "daily automated database backups" is contradicted by the operational record. 30-day retention is unverifiable from the supplied materials because the backup pipeline is non-functional.

---

**Finding 4 (claim 4): Platform-level redundancy and automatic failover — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:18): "platform-level redundancy and automatic failover." doc9:5: "The system has redundancy and automatic failover through Heroku's platform-level process management."

Evidence: doc4:5 — single dyno: `standard-1x` (1 GB RAM, 0.5 CPU). doc4:6 — database `heroku-postgresql:standard-0` "running on the same dyno as the application." doc4:7 — "Read Replicas: None." doc4:8 — "Separate DB Instance: No."

Gap: There is exactly one application process and the database co-located on it. No second dyno, no read replica, no separate DB instance. A failure of the single dyno takes down both application and data layer simultaneously. "Redundancy" and "automatic failover" do not exist in the current configuration.

---

**Finding 5 (claim 5): 99.9% uptime monitoring — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:19): "99.9% uptime monitoring." doc9:6: "We monitor uptime at 99.9%."

Evidence: doc4:22 — "Uptime Monitor: None (No Pingdom, UptimeRobot, or custom checks)." doc4:23 — "Status Page: Heroku built-in status page only."

Gap: No uptime monitoring of any kind is configured. The Heroku platform status page reports on Heroku infrastructure, not on application-level availability. The claim that uptime is "monitored" is contradicted by the absence of any monitoring tool or custom check.

Evidence: doc4:5 — single `standard-1x` dyno, 1 GB RAM, 0.5 CPU. doc4:6 — DB co-located on the same dyno. doc4:7-8 — no read replicas, no separate DB instance.

Gap: Heroku does permit adding dynos via the dashboard, so the one-click mechanism exists in principle. However, the database resides on the same dyno as the application; true horizontal scaling requires moving the DB to a separate instance (a manual reconfiguration, not a one-click operation). The 1 GB / 0.5 CPU constraint is far below what an analytics platform serving 97 accounts would need under elevated load. "Automatic scaling" does not occur by default on standard plans; the claim describes an operating mode the system is not configured for.

---

**Finding 7 (claim 7): Comprehensive test coverage across critical paths — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:21): "comprehensive test coverage across critical paths." doc9:7: "The codebase is well-documented with comprehensive test coverage across all critical paths."

Gap: Twelve unit tests confined to `test/utils/`, zero integration tests, and zero payment-path tests cannot constitute "comprehensive test coverage across critical paths." The payment path (Stripe billing, $16,000/mo of subscription revenue) has no test coverage. There is no CI pipeline to run even the 12 tests on commit.

**Finding 8 (claim 8): Minimal operational overhead; turnkey acquisition — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:9): "minimal operational overhead… This is a turnkey acquisition opportunity."

Evidence: doc4:17-19 — backups failing 21 days, no alerting. doc4:22 — no uptime monitoring. doc6:12-16 — 23 phantom accounts with no explanation. doc3:25-31 — no CI/CD, no staging environment, no branch protection, no code review. doc4:28 — "DNS Management: Managed personally by 'dave'. No secondary DNS provider." doc4:29 — secrets in plain Heroku config vars, no vault. doc7:42-45 — 15 Pro accounts with no signed ToS on file. doc5:19 — $24,000/mo enterprise revenue collected via manual wire transfer.

Gap: "Turnkey" implies the buyer can operate the system as-is. The evidence shows a failing backup pipeline, zero monitoring, DNS bound to the departing owner's personal account, no deployment safety rails, unexplained phantom accounts, and a third of revenue collected by manual wire. Immediate remediation across multiple domains is required before the system is operable.

**Finding 9 (claim 9): All third-party integrations on standard SaaS agreements; no proprietary lock-in — [delta]**

content:
**Finding 1 (claim 1): 120 "active accounts" contradicted by 23 phantom accounts — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:9, doc1:13): "a loyal customer base of 120 active accounts" / "Active Customers: 120"

Evidence: doc6:3 — "Total Accounts Marked 'Active': 120." doc6:7 — 94 Stripe-linked. doc6:10 — 3 enterprise wire-transfer. doc6:12–16 — "Phantom/Inactive Accounts: 23 … Created in Q1 2026. No payment events in the last 90 days. Last login dates: 60–120 days ago. No notes or memos on file regarding creation or non-payment." doc6:18 — "All 120 accounts are currently marked as 'active' in the CRM."

Gap: 23 of the 120 (19%) have no payment events in 90 days and no login in 60–120 days. The paying, engaged base is 97 (94 Stripe + 3 enterprise). The listing overstates the active customer count by 24%.

**Finding 2 (claim 2): "Low churn / stable base" contradicted by 23 dormant accounts and no churn metric — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:9, doc1:14): "low churn" / "Churn: Low (stable base of recurring subscribers)"

Evidence: doc6:12–16 — 23 phantom accounts created Q1 2026, zero payment events in 90 days, last logins 60–120 days ago. doc7:37–39 — 8 pilot agreements with "No payment obligation," expiring Q3 2026. No churn rate, cohort table, or retention metric appears in any supplied document.

Gap: 19% of the claimed customer base went from creation to zero-payment within ~18 months. No churn figure is documented anywhere. The only available indicator (23 dormant of 120) points to elevated attrition, not low churn.

**Finding 3 (claims 3): Daily backup schedule configured but failing for 21 consecutive days — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:19, doc9:10): "daily automated database backups with 30-day retention" / "The database is backed up daily to Heroku's managed storage with 30-day retention."

Evidence: doc4:16 — "Schedule: Daily at 2:00 AM via `heroku pg:backups schedule`" confirms the schedule exists. doc4:17 — "Status: Failures recorded for the last 21 days." doc4:18 — "Last Successful Backup: 2026-07-30." doc4:19 — "Alerting: None configured for backup failures."

Gap: The daily schedule is configured, satisfying the literal claim. However, backups have failed every day for 21 days prior to the materials date. No alerting exists, so failures went undetected. The 30-day retention claim cannot be verified because the most recent usable backup predates the failure window; whether 30 days of retained snapshots still exist on Heroku's managed storage is unknown from the materials.

**Finding 4 (claim 4): "Platform-level redundancy and automatic failover" contradicted by single-dyno, co-located architecture — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:18, doc2:3, doc9:5): "platform-level redundancy and automatic failover" / "automatic scaling and failover capabilities at the platform level" / "redundancy and automatic failover through Heroku's process management."

Evidence: doc4:5 — "Dyno: `standard-1x` (1GB RAM, 0.5 CPU)" — a single dyno. doc4:6 — "Database: `heroku-postgresql:standard-0` (running on the same dyno as the application)." doc4:7 — "Read Replicas: None." doc4:8 — "Separate DB Instance: No."

Gap: Redundancy requires at least two independent execution points. The deployment is one dyno with the database co-located on it. Heroku restarts a crashed process, but there is no redundant compute, no separate database, and no failover path. The description of the architecture in doc2:3 ("redundancy") is contradicted by the infrastructure in doc4:5–8.

**Finding 5 (claim 5): 99.9% uptime monitoring does not exist — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:19, doc9:6): "99.9% uptime monitoring" / "We monitor uptime at 99.9%."

Evidence: doc4:22 — "Uptime Monitor: None (No Pingdom, UptimeRobot, or custom checks)." doc4:23 — "Status Page: Heroku built-in status page only."

Gap: No uptime monitoring of any kind is in place. The 99.9% figure appears in three enterprise SLAs (doc7:8, doc7:16, doc7:24) as a contractual obligation with service-credit penalties, but no mechanism exists to measure it. The claim that uptime is "monitored at 99.9%" is false.

**Finding 6 (claim 6): "Automatic scaling / no manual intervention" not supported by single-dyno configuration — [partial]**

Claim (doc2:3, doc9:8): "automatic scaling … no manual intervention required" / "adding dynos is a one-click operation in the Heroku dashboard."

Evidence: doc4:5 — single `standard-1x` dyno (1 GB RAM, 0.5 CPU). doc4:6 — DB co-located on the same dyno. Heroku's one-click dyno addition (doc9:8) is a dashboard operation requiring manual action; it is not automatic scaling. No auto-scaling policy or `WEB_CONCURRENCY` tuning evidence appears in doc4. The standard-1x plan is a fixed-resource instance, not an elastic auto-scaling tier.

Gap: The seller's doc9:8 statement ("one-click operation") is technically true of Heroku's dashboard, but the seller's doc2:3 statement ("automatic scaling … no manual intervention") is not supported. A single standard-1x dyno does not scale automatically. The buyer must add dynos manually and reconfigure the database relationship.

**Finding 7 (claim 7): "Comprehensive test coverage across critical paths" contradicted by 12 unit tests, zero integration, zero payment tests — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:21, doc9:7): "Well-documented codebase with comprehensive test coverage across critical paths" / "comprehensive test coverage across all critical paths."

Evidence: doc3:27 — "Unit Tests: 12 (all located in `test/utils/`)." doc3:28 — "Integration Tests: 0." doc3:29 — "Payment-Path Tests: 0." doc3:25 — "CI/CD Pipeline: None configured." doc3:30 — "Staging Environment: None." doc3:31 — "Branch Protection: None."

Gap: Twelve unit tests in a `test/utils/` directory with zero integration tests and zero payment-path tests cannot be characterized as "comprehensive coverage across critical paths." The payment path (doc5, doc8:3–5), authentication (doc3:14 — `auth/` is 47% of dave's commits), and enterprise data flows have no test coverage. No CI/CD or staging environment exists to run what tests are present.

**Finding 8 (claim 8): "Minimal operational overhead / turnkey acquisition" contradicted by absent CI/CD, monitoring, alerting, and single-person DNS — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:9): "minimal operational overhead" / "turnkey acquisition."

Evidence: doc3:25 — no CI/CD. doc3:30 — no staging. doc3:31–32 — no branch protection or code review. doc4:17–19 — backups failing 21 days with no alerting. doc4:22 — no uptime monitoring. doc4:28 — DNS managed personally by 'dave', no secondary provider. doc4:29 — no secrets vault; 14 config vars. doc8:29–32 — GoDaddy risk: "If domain expires or GoDaddy has an issue, the app is unreachable."

Gap: The buyer inherits a system with no CI/CD, no staging, no monitoring, no backup alerting, a single-person DNS dependency, and a secrets-management gap. These are individually addressable but collectively represent a substantial initial remediation burden, contradicting "minimal operational overhead" and "turnkey."

**Finding 9 (claim 9): "No proprietary lock-in" qualified by DataEnrich.io dependency, Google OAuth single point, and dave-personal DNS — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:22, doc9:9): "All third-party integrations are on standard SaaS agreements with no proprietary lock-in" / "no lock-in."

Evidence: doc8:8–12 — DataEnrich.io: 90-day termination notice either party, 40% of features depend on the API, "Fallback: None implemented. If API is down or pricing changes, product degrades to basic mode (no enrichment)." doc8:28 — Google OAuth: "No contractual relationship." doc4:28 / doc8:31 — DNS managed personally by 'dave', no secondary provider.

Gap: Most integrations are standard SaaS (Stripe, Heroku, Redis, Twilio). Three dependencies deviate: DataEnrich.io carries functional lock-in (no fallback, 90-day exit, 40% feature dependency); Google OAuth has no contract and is an authentication single point; DNS is personally held by the seller with no redundancy. The blanket "no lock-in" claim is substantially true for payment and hosting but false for the product-intelligence and DNS layers.

**Finding 10 (claim 10): Blended MRR $40,000 — arithmetic supported, composition carries risk — [real, operational caveat]**

Claim (doc1:12): "Blended MRR: $40,000."

Evidence: doc5:17 — "Total Stripe MRR: $16,000." doc5:19 — "3 enterprise companies … $8,000/mo each, paid via wire transfer." $16,000 + 3 × $8,000 = $40,000. Arithmetic confirmed.

Derived: Enterprise revenue concentration
  Basis: doc5:17 — $16,000 Stripe MRR; doc5:19 — $24,000 wire-transfer enterprise MRR.
  Derivation: $24,000 / $40,000 = 60% of MRR from 3 wire contracts.
  Consequence: 60% of stated MRR flows outside Stripe with no transaction-level audit trail in the supplied materials. The buyer cannot verify wire payments from the data room alone.

Gap: None to the arithmetic. The operational caveat is that $24,000/mo (60%) is wire-transfer revenue with no Stripe-level traceability, and GlobalMart's contract renews 2026-11-01 (doc7:13), approximately two months after the materials date.

**Finding 11 (claim 11): Asking $480,000 at 12× MRR — arithmetic correct — [real]**

Claim (doc1:5): "Asking Price: $480,000 (12x blended MRR)."

Evidence: doc1:12 — MRR $40,000. 12 × $40,000 = $480,000. Arithmetic confirmed. The asking price is self-consistent with the stated MRR figure.

Gap: None. The multiple is arithmetically correct. Whether $40,000 MRR and the resulting multiple are appropriate for a $480k transaction is a pricing decision for the buyer, not an accuracy claim about the listing.

**Finding 12 (claim 12): Mix of enterprise and month-to-month subscribers confirmed — [real]**

Claim (doc1:9, doc1:15): "a mix of high-value enterprise contracts and a broad base of month-to-month subscribers."

Evidence: doc7:3–27 — three enterprise contracts at $8,000/mo (Acme, GlobalMart, ShopStream). doc7:29–33 — 94 month-to-month Pro subscriptions at $149/mo with auto-renewal. doc5:8–10 — 91 Pro accounts at $149/mo in Stripe.

Gap: None.

**Finding 13 (claim 13): Recurring subscription (monthly and annual enterprise) confirmed — [real]**

Claim (doc1:15): "Revenue Model: Recurring subscription (Monthly & Annual Enterprise)."

Evidence: doc7:4, doc7:13, doc7:21 — enterprise contracts are annual terms with renewal dates. doc7:30–32 — month-to-month subscriptions auto-renew with no-penalty cancellation. doc5:4 — 94 active Stripe subscriptions.

Gap: None.

**Finding 14 (claim 14): Recurring-revenue SaaS model confirmed — [real]**

Claim (doc1:9): "recurring-revenue SaaS platform."

Evidence: doc5:4 — 94 active recurring subscriptions. doc7:3–27 — annual enterprise contracts. doc5:19 — monthly wire payments from enterprise clients. The revenue structure is recurring subscription in both Stripe and wire components.

Gap: None.

**Finding 15 (claim 15): Customer range from independent merchants to enterprise retailers confirmed — [real]**

Claim (doc1:9): "ranging from independent merchants to mid-market enterprise retailers."

Evidence: doc5:9–10 — 91 Pro accounts at $149/mo (independent-merchant tier). doc7:5, 13, 21 — Acme Retail, GlobalMart, ShopStream at $8,000/mo (enterprise tier). doc7:37–40 — 8 pilot accounts (trial/early-merchant stage).

Gap: None.

**Finding 16 (claim 16): Immediate cash flow confirmed but 60% is wire without Stripe audit trail — [real, operational caveat]**

Claim (doc1:9): "immediate cash flow."

Evidence: doc5:17 — $16,000/mo in Stripe (automated, recurring). doc5:19 / doc7:3–27 — $24,000/mo via wire transfer from 3 enterprise clients. Monthly cash flow of $40,000 is present.

Derived: Wire-transfer share of cash flow
  Basis: doc5:17 — $16,000 Stripe MRR; doc5:19 — $24,000 enterprise wire MRR.
  Derivation: $24,000 / $40,000 = 60% of monthly cash flow received outside Stripe.
  Consequence: The buyer cannot confirm wire-payment regularity, counterparty identity, or late-payment behaviour from Stripe exports alone. The materials do not include bank statements or wire-transfer receipts.

Gap: None to the existence of cash flow. The operational caveat is the wire-transfer concentration and the absence of bank-level evidence in the data room.

**Finding 17 (claim 17): Analytics product exists but "real-time" depends on an external API with no fallback — [real, operational caveat]**

Claim (doc1:9): "real-time analytics and product intelligence to e-commerce sellers."

Evidence: doc2:5 — third-party data enrichment API provides product data. doc8:8–12 — DataEnrich.io provides product matching, price comparison, category classification; 40% of features depend on it; "Fallback: None implemented. If API is down or pricing changes, product degrades to basic mode (no enrichment)." doc4:5 — single standard-1x dyno constrains concurrent processing capacity.

Gap: The product does deliver analytics and product intelligence, satisfying the core of the claim. The "real-time" qualifier depends on DataEnrich.io availability; if the API is down or reprices, the product degrades to a no-enrichment mode (doc8:12) with no documented degradation path or caching layer.

**Finding 18 (claim 18): Third-party data-enrichment API integration confirmed — [real]**

Claim (doc2:5): "we integrate with a third-party data enrichment API that provides real-time product data."

Evidence: doc8:8 — "DataEnrich.io … Function: Product data enrichment API (product matching, price comparison, category classification)." doc8:9 — "$400/mo flat." doc8:11 — "40% of features depend on this API." The integration exists and supplies product data to the platform.

Gap: None. The integration is confirmed. (The "real-time" characterisation is addressed under Finding 17.)

**Finding 19 (claim 19): Stripe payment processing confirmed, but 60% of revenue bypasses Stripe — [real, minor caveat]**

Claim (doc1:20, doc2:5): "secure payment processing via Stripe" / "Payment processing is securely handled through Stripe."

Evidence: doc5:4 — 94 active Stripe subscriptions totalling $16,000 MRR. doc8:3–5 — Stripe handles payment processing at 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction. doc5:19 — "These [enterprise wire] payments are not processed through Stripe and are not included in the $16,000 MRR figure above."

Gap: Stripe does process payments (94 subscriptions), satisfying the claim. The minor caveat is that $24,000/mo in enterprise revenue (60% of MRR) flows via wire transfer outside Stripe, so "payment processing via Stripe" covers $16,000/mo, not the full $40,000/mo stated in the listing.

**Finding 20 (claim 20): Stripe supports credit-card transactions and recurring billing — [real]**

Claim (doc2:5): "Stripe, which supports both credit card transactions and recurring billing."

Evidence: doc5:4–17 — 94 active recurring subscriptions processed through Stripe (recurring billing confirmed). doc8:4–5 — Stripe handles credit-card payment processing at 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction. Stripe's documented functionality includes both credit-card authorisation and recurring/subscription billing.

Gap: None.

**Finding 1 (claim 3): Backup schedule configured but 21 consecutive days of failures, no alerting, 30-day retention not evidenced — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:19; doc9:6; doc9:10; doc2:5): "daily automated database backups with 30-day retention"; "maintain daily automated database backups"; "The database is backed up daily to Heroku's managed storage with 30-day retention"; "configured with daily scheduled backups to ensure data integrity and recoverability."

Evidence: doc4:16 — "Schedule: Daily at 2:00 AM via `heroku pg:backups schedule`" (the daily schedule exists). doc4:17 — "Status: Failures recorded for the last 21 days." doc4:18 — "Last Successful Backup: 2026-07-30." doc4:19 — "Alerting: None configured for backup failures."

Derived: Backup-gap window at as-of date 2026-08-31
  Basis: doc4:18 — "Last Successful Backup: 2026-07-30"
         doc4:17 — "Failures recorded for the last 21 days."
  Derivation: 2026-07-30 to 2026-08-31 = 32 calendar days without a confirmed successful backup. The 21 failure records are a subset; the gap from last success is 32 days.
  Consequence: For a SaaS whose enterprise clients hold 99.9 % SLAs with service-credit remedies (doc7:9, 18, 25), a 32-day backup gap means any catastrophic data-loss event would destroy revenue-generating records with no recoverable snapshot within the contractual SLA window. The buyer inherits this risk from day one.

Gap: The daily schedule is configured, so the claim is substantially true in intent. The material gaps are (a) 21 consecutive days of failures with no alerting, (b) the 30-day retention period is not evidenced in the supplied infrastructure configuration, and (c) the 32-day window since last confirmed backup exceeds the 30-day retention the seller states, making the retention claim moot if a loss occurred before the last successful run.

---

**Finding 2 (claim 4): Single dyno, database co-located, no read replicas — no redundancy or failover exists — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:18; doc9:5; doc2:3; doc2:5): "platform-level redundancy and automatic failover"; "The system has redundancy and automatic failover through Heroku's platform-level process management"; "Heroku, which provides automatic scaling and failover capabilities at the platform level"; "standard SaaS stack with platform-level redundancy."

Gap: The claim asserts redundancy and automatic failover. The evidence shows one standard-1x web dyno with the PostgreSQL instance running inside it, zero read replicas, and no separate database instance. Heroku's process manager restarts a crashed dyno, but a single dyno provides no redundancy, and co-locating the database means a dyno failure takes both the application and the data service. "Failover" requires a second instance to fail over to; none exists. The claim is contradicted by the supplied infrastructure.

---

**Finding 3 (claim 1): 120 "active" accounts include 23 phantom/inactive accounts; true active base is 97 — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:9; doc1:13): "We have built a loyal customer base of 120 active accounts"; "Active Customers: 120."

Evidence: doc6:3 — "Total Accounts Marked 'Active': 120." doc6:12–16 — "Phantom/Inactive Accounts: 23 … Created in Q1 2026 … No payment events in the last 90 days … Last login dates: 60–120 days ago … No notes or memos on file regarding creation or non-payment." doc6:18 — "All 120 accounts are currently marked as 'active' in the CRM." doc5:4 — "Total Active Subscriptions: 94." doc6:6 — "Stripe-Linked Accounts: 94." doc7:3 — "Enterprise Contracts (3)."

Derived: True active-account count
  Basis: doc6:6 — 94 Stripe-linked
         doc7:3 — 3 enterprise wire-transfer accounts
  Derivation: 94 + 3 = 97 accounts with confirmed payment relationships. 120 − 97 = 23 phantom accounts.
  Consequence: The buyer's revenue per account, customer-count metrics, and the "loyal base" narrative are overstated by 24 %. The $480,000 asking price is derived from $40,000 MRR across 120 accounts; the actual paying base is 97.

Gap: The CRM status field shows 120, but 23 accounts have no payment events in 90 days and no login in 60–120 days. The claim of "120 active accounts" is contradicted; 97 accounts have demonstrable payment activity.

**Finding 4 (claim 5): No uptime monitoring is configured; "99.9% uptime monitoring" is not implemented — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:19; doc9:6): "99.9% uptime monitoring"; "We monitor uptime at 99.9%."

Evidence: doc4:22 — "Uptime Monitor: None (No Pingdom, UptimeRobot, or custom checks)." doc4:23 — "Status Page: Heroku built-in status page only."

Evidence of absence:
  Lexical search: terms "uptime," "monitor," "Pingdom," "UptimeRobot," "health check," "status page," "availability" across all supplied documents. Result: doc4:22 explicitly states "None." No other document records an uptime-monitoring configuration.
  Structural search: inspected doc4 (infrastructure config) for monitoring, alerting, and observability sections. Only entries found are the Heroku built-in status page (doc4:23) and "Alerting: None configured for backup failures" (doc4:19). No external monitoring service is referenced anywhere in the data room.

Gap: The claim states uptime is "monitored at 99.9 %." No uptime-monitoring tool or process is configured. The Heroku status page reports platform-level events, not the FlowMetrics application's availability. The buyer cannot verify SLA compliance (required by three enterprise contracts, doc7:9/18/25) because no measurement infrastructure exists.

---

**Finding 5 (claim 8): "Minimal operational overhead" and "turnkey acquisition" contradicted by absent monitoring, CI/CD, backups, DNS redundancy, and secrets management — [delta]**

No secondary DNS provider." doc4:29 — "14 secrets stored in Heroku config vars … No secrets vault." doc3:22 — "Commits in Last 30 Days: 0."

Gap: At least seven decision-relevant operational controls are absent or broken (backup integrity, uptime monitoring, CI/CD, integration/payment testing, staging, branch protection, DNS redundancy, secrets vault). These are not individually exotic; collectively they mean the buyer cannot operate the business as claimed without substantial remediation across infrastructure, process, and security. "Turnkey" implies the buyer can take the keys and run; the supplied state requires building the operational layer.

---

**Finding 6 (claim 9): "No proprietary lock-in" contradicted by undocumented OAuth dependency, 40 %-of-features API with no fallback, and personal DNS — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:22; doc9:9): "All third-party integrations are on standard SaaS agreements with no proprietary lock-in."

If API is down or pricing changes, product degrades to basic mode (no enrichment)." doc4:28 — "DNS Management: Managed personally by 'dave'. No secondary DNS provider." doc8:29–32 — "GoDaddy … If domain expires or GoDaddy has an issue, the app is unreachable."

Gap: Most integrations (Stripe, Heroku, Redis, Twilio) are standard SaaS. The claim is substantially true for those. However, Google OAuth operates with "no contractual relationship" (doc8:28); DataEnrich.io, which 40 % of product features depend on, has "Fallback: None implemented" (doc8:12); and DNS is a single-person, single-provider arrangement (doc4:28). These three dependencies create effective lock-in or critical single points of failure that the "no lock-in" characterization omits.

---

**Finding 7 (claim 10): Blended MRR of $40,000: arithmetic consistent, but $24,000 (60 %) from wire-transfer enterprise contracts not independently verifiable — [real, minor caveat]**

Claim (doc1:9; doc1:12): "Our blended Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) stands at $40,000"; "Blended MRR: $40,000."

Evidence: doc5:5 — "Total MRR (Stripe): $16,000." doc5:19 — "3 enterprise companies … separate contracts for $8,000/mo each, paid via wire transfer. These payments are not processed through Stripe and are not included in the $16,000 MRR figure above." doc7:5, 14, 22 — each enterprise contract listed at $8,000/mo.

Derived: Blended MRR reconciliation
  Basis: doc5:5 — "$16,000" (Stripe)
         doc7:5/14/22 — 3 × "$8,000/mo" (wire)
  Derivation: $16,000 + (3 × $8,000) = $40,000.
  Consequence: The stated blended MRR is arithmetically consistent with the two revenue sources the seller documents. However, 60 % of the total rests on wire-transfer contracts whose payment receipt is evidenced only by the seller's own contracts summary; no bank statements or payment-confirmation documents are supplied. The buyer should verify collection independently.

Gap: The $16,000 Stripe MRR is independently confirmed by the Stripe export. The $24,000 wire-transfer component is asserted in doc5:19 and doc7 but not corroborated by a third-party payment record. The claim holds on the seller's own figures; the caveat is the absence of independent payment evidence for the majority component.

---

**Finding 8 (claim 11): $480,000 asking price = 12 × $40,000; arithmetic correct — [real]**

Claim (doc1:5): "Asking Price: $480,000 (12x blended MRR)."

Evidence: doc1:12 — "Blended MRR: $40,000."

Derived: Multiple verification
  Basis: doc1:5 — "$480,000"
         doc1:12 — "$40,000"
  Derivation: $480,000 ÷ $40,000 = 12.0.
  Consequence: The stated multiple is arithmetically accurate against the stated MRR. Whether 12× is an appropriate multiple for this asset is a transaction decision outside the audit's scope.

Gap: None. The arithmetic is correct. (The accuracy of the underlying $40,000 figure is addressed in Finding 7.)

---

**Finding 9 (claim 6): Horizontal scaling is mechanically possible but architecturally blocked by co-located database and single-dyno configuration — [partial]**

Claim (doc9:8; doc2:3): "The stack is designed to scale horizontally — adding dynos is a one-click operation in the Heroku dashboard"; "automatic scaling and failover capabilities at the platform level … remains available even under varying load conditions, with no manual intervention required."

Evidence: doc4:5 — "Dyno: `standard-1x` (1GB RAM, 0.5 CPU)" (single dyno). doc4:6 — "Database: `heroku-postgresql:standard-0` (running on the same dyno as the application)." doc4:7 — "Read Replicas: None." doc8:13–14 — "Heroku … Cost: $25/mo (standard-1x dyno)."

Gap: Adding web dynos through the Heroku dashboard is mechanically a click (the claim is true in the narrow mechanical sense). The claim fails architecturally: the database runs inside the same dyno, so additional web dynos do not relieve the primary load bottleneck, and the `standard-0` plan provides no connection pooling for multi-dyno operation. "Automatic scaling" is not configured; Heroku's Auto-Scale add-on requires a performance-tier dyno and explicit enablement. "No manual intervention required for routine operations" is contradicted by the current single-dyno, shared-DB topology, under which load increases require manual DB migration before additional dynos would help.

---

**Finding 10 (claim 7): "Comprehensive test coverage across critical paths" contradicted by 12 utility-only unit tests, zero integration, zero payment-path — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:21; doc9:7): "comprehensive test coverage across critical paths"; "The codebase is well-documented with comprehensive test coverage across all critical paths."

Evidence: doc3:27 — "Unit Tests: 12 (all located in `test/utils/`)." doc3:28 — "Integration Tests: 0." doc3:29 — "Payment-Path Tests: 0." doc3:14 — "`auth/`: 47%" of dave's commits (highest-activity directory). doc3:25 — "CI/CD Pipeline: None configured." doc3:30 — "Staging Environment: None."

Gap: The claim of "comprehensive test coverage across critical paths" is contradicted. Critical paths identified by commit frequency (`auth/`, 47 % of development effort) and by revenue function (payment processing, 3 enterprise SLAs) have zero tests. The only tests present are 12 unit tests in `test/utils/`, a directory that is not a revenue-critical path. No CI/CD pipeline exists to enforce even those 12 tests on commits. The "all critical paths" wording is directly refuted by the 0/0 counts for integration and payment-path tests.

---

**Finding 11 (claim 2): "Low churn; stable recurring subscribers" — 23 phantom accounts and 8 expiring pilots create material doubt; no churn rate supplied — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:9; doc1:14): "The business operates with low churn"; "Churn: Low (stable base of recurring subscribers)."

Evidence: doc6:12–16 — 23 phantom accounts created Q1 2026, no payment in 90 days, last login 60–120 days ago. doc7:36–40 — 8 pilot agreements expiring Q3 2026 with "Payment Obligation: None." doc3:22 — "Commits in Last 30 Days: 0" (no product engagement activity). No churn-rate document exists in the data room.

Evidence of absence:
  Lexical search: terms "churn," "attrition," "cancellation rate," "cohort retention" across all supplied documents. Result: doc1:14 states "Churn: Low" as an assertion only. No quantitative churn figure, cohort analysis, or cancellation log is present.
  Structural search: inspected doc5 (Stripe export) for cancellation or expired-subscription counts; inspected doc6 (CRM export) for status-change history; inspected doc3 (git history) for retention telemetry. None contain churn metrics.

Gap: The seller asserts "low churn" but supplies no churn rate. The 23 phantom accounts (19 % of the claimed base) with no payment in 90 days and the 8 pilots expiring Q3 2026 with no payment obligation create a material gap in the "stable base" characterization. The claim is not directly contradicted by a measured high-churn rate, but the evidence pattern is inconsistent with "low churn" without further data. The buyer should request a 12-month cohort retention report before closing.

---

**Finding 12 (claim 12): Enterprise and month-to-month mix confirmed — [real]**

Claim (doc1:9): "driven by a mix of high-value enterprise contracts and a broad base of month-to-month subscribers."

Evidence: doc7:3–27 — 3 enterprise contracts at $8,000/mo (annual terms). doc7:29–33 — 94 month-to-month Pro subscriptions, auto-renewal. doc5:9 — 91 Pro accounts at $149/mo.

Claim (doc1:15): "Revenue Model: Recurring subscription (Monthly & Annual Enterprise)."

Evidence: doc7:29–32 — "Auto-renewal" month-to-month. doc7:5–8, 13–16, 21–24 — enterprise contracts with annual terms and renewal dates. doc5:3–4 — 94 active recurring subscriptions.

**Finding 14 (claim 14): Recurring-revenue SaaS confirmed; caveat on wire-transfer collection and 8 free pilots — [real, minor caveat]**

Claim (doc1:9): "revenue-positive, recurring-revenue SaaS platform."

Evidence: doc5:3–4 — 94 active subscriptions (automated recurring). doc7:5–27 — 3 annual enterprise contracts. doc7:36–40 — 8 pilots, "Payment Obligation: None," "Expiration: Q3 2026." doc5:19 — enterprise revenue via wire transfer, not automated billing.

Gap: The model is recurring-revenue SaaS. The minor caveat: 60 % of MRR ($24,000 of $40,000) is collected via manual wire transfer rather than automated subscription billing, and 8 accounts on free pilots expire Q3 2026 with no revenue obligation. The characterization holds but the revenue mix is less fully automated than "recurring-revenue SaaS" implies.

**Finding 15 (claim 15): Customer range from independent merchants to enterprise confirmed; "mid-market" not independently verified — [real, minor caveat]**

Claim (doc1:9): "ranging from independent merchants to mid-market enterprise retailers."

Evidence: doc5:9 — 91 Pro subscribers at $149/mo (consistent with independent/small merchants). doc7:5/14/22 — 3 enterprise clients at $8,000/mo (Acme Retail, GlobalMart, ShopStream). No customer-size segmentation document is supplied.

Gap: The $149/mo-to-$8,000/mo spectrum confirms a range from small merchants to enterprise-scale clients. "Mid-market" is a characterization applied to the three named enterprise clients; no revenue-band or employee-count evidence in the data room independently supports or refutes the "mid-market" label. The claim is not contradicted; the specific "mid-market" qualifier is unverified.

Claim (doc1:9): "immediate cash flow."

Gap: None. The business generates recurring monthly revenue through both automated (Stripe) and contract (wire) channels. "Immediate cash flow" is consistent with the revenue evidence, subject to the wire-transfer verification caveat in Finding 7.

---

**Finding 17 (claim 17): Real-time analytics and product intelligence provided; "real-time" qualified by single-API dependency with no fallback — [real, operational caveat]**

Claim (doc1:9): "providing real-time analytics and product intelligence to e-commerce sellers."

Evidence: doc2:5 — "third-party data enrichment API that provides real-time product data." doc8:7–9 — DataEnrich.io provides "product matching, price comparison, category classification." doc7:11/19/27 — enterprise required features include product matching, price comparison, real-time inventory sync, category classification. doc8:12 — "Fallback: None implemented. If API is down or pricing changes, product degrades to basic mode (no enrichment)."

Gap: The platform does deliver analytics and product intelligence. The operational caveat: all "real-time" enrichment functionality depends entirely on DataEnrich.io with no fallback (doc8:12). If that API is unavailable, the product degrades to basic mode. The claim holds under current conditions but the buyer should budget for redundancy or a second data source before relying on the "real-time" label for SLA commitments (doc7:9/18/25 require 99.9 % / 99.5 % uptime).

**Finding 18 (claim 18): DataEnrich.io is the third-party data-enrichment API supplying product data — [real]**

content:
**Finding 1 (claim 1): Active customer count — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:13): "Active Customers: 120"

Evidence: doc6:3 — "Total Accounts Marked 'Active': 120"; doc6:12-16 — "Phantom/Inactive Accounts: 23. Created in Q1 2026. No payment events in the last 90 days. Last login dates: 60-120 days ago. No notes or memos on file regarding creation or non-payment." doc6:6-7 — 94 Stripe-linked accounts plus 3 enterprise wire-transfer accounts.

Gap: The CRM field reads 120, but 23 of those accounts have no payment events in 90 days and last logins 60–120 days ago (doc6:14-15). Genuinely paying accounts number 97 (94 Stripe + 3 wire). The "active" characterisation overstates the paying base by roughly 19%.

**Finding 2 (claim 2): Low churn / stable recurring base — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:14): "Churn: Low (stable base of recurring subscribers)"

Evidence: doc6:12-16 — 23 accounts with no payment events in 90 days, no explanatory notes. doc7:36-38 — 8 pilot agreements with "Payment Obligation: None" expiring Q3 2026. No explicit churn-rate figure appears in any supplied document.

Gap: The claim is not contradicted by a measured churn rate (none was supplied), but the 23 accounts with no payment events and no notes (doc6:14-16) plus 8 expiring zero-obligation pilots (doc7:37-38) leave the "stable" characterisation unsupported and directionally concerning.

**Finding 3 (claim 3): Daily automated database backups — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:19): "daily automated database backups"; doc9:10: "The database is backed up daily to Heroku's managed storage with 30-day retention."

Evidence: doc4:16 — "Schedule: Daily at 2:00 AM via `heroku pg:backups schedule`." doc4:17 — "Failures recorded for the last 21 days." doc4:18 — "Last Successful Backup: 2026-07-30." doc4:19 — "Alerting: None configured for backup failures."

Gap: The daily automated schedule exists and is configured (doc4:16), confirming the automation. However, backups have been failing for 21 consecutive days (doc4:17) with the last successful run on 2026-07-30 (doc4:18), and no alerting would surface the failures (doc4:19). The schedule is automated but has not been executing.

**Finding 4 (claim 4): Platform-level redundancy and automatic failover — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:18): "platform-level redundancy and automatic failover"; doc9:5: "redundancy and automatic failover through Heroku's platform-level process management."

Evidence: doc4:5 — "Dyno: `standard-1x` (1GB RAM, 0.5 CPU)." doc4:6 — "Database: `heroku-postgresql:standard-0` (running on the same dyno as the application)." doc4:7 — "Read Replicas: None." doc4:8 — "Separate DB Instance: No."

Gap: The application and database run on a single dyno with no read replica, no separate database instance, and no second web dyno. Heroku's process-management restart of a crashed dyno is basic orchestration, not redundancy. There is no instance to fail over to; a dyno-level failure (disk, host) takes the entire system down. The claim of redundancy and failover is contradicted by the single-instance, co-located-database topology.

**Finding 5 (claim 5): 99.9% uptime monitoring — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:19): "99.9% uptime monitoring"; doc9:6: "We monitor uptime at 99.9%."

Evidence: doc4:22 — "Uptime Monitor: None (No Pingdom, UptimeRobot, or custom checks)." doc4:23 — "Status Page: Heroku built-in status page only." Lexical search: no uptime-monitoring service named in doc4 or doc8. Structural search: doc4 "Monitoring" section contains only the above two lines; no additional monitoring configuration exists in the infrastructure doc.

Gap: No uptime monitoring of any kind is configured (doc4:22). The 99.9% figure is an unmeasured target, not a monitored and reported metric. The claim of active monitoring is contradicted.

**Finding 6 (claim 6): Automatic scaling, availability under varying load, no manual intervention — [delta]**

Claim (doc2:3): "automatic scaling and failover capabilities at the platform level. This ensures that the application remains available even under varying load conditions, with no manual intervention required for routine operations."

Evidence: doc4:5 — single `standard-1x` dyno. doc4:6 — database co-located on the same dyno. doc4:7-8 — no read replicas, no separate DB instance. doc4:22 — no uptime monitoring to detect load issues. doc3:25 — no CI/CD pipeline (manual deploy).

Gap: A single dyno with a co-located database cannot scale horizontally under load; the database is the bottleneck and shares the dyno's single CPU and 1 GB RAM. A dyno restart for any reason (deploy, OOM, host maintenance) interrupts both application and database. The "automatic scaling" and "remains available under varying load" claims are contradicted by the single-dyno, co-located-DB configuration. Heroku does restart a crashed dyno, but that is process management, not scaling or failover.

**Finding 7 (claim 7): Comprehensive test coverage across critical paths — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:21): "comprehensive test coverage across critical paths"; doc9:7: "comprehensive test coverage across all critical paths."

Evidence: doc3:27 — "Unit Tests: 12 (all located in `test/utils/`)." doc3:28 — "Integration Tests: 0." doc3:29 — "Payment-Path Tests: 0." doc3:25 — "CI/CD Pipeline: None configured." doc3:30 — "Staging Environment: None."

Gap: Twelve unit tests in a single `test/utils/` directory, zero integration tests, and zero payment-path tests (doc3:27-29) are not comprehensive coverage of critical paths. The auth module accounts for 47% of commits (doc3:14) yet has no dedicated test suite noted. The claim is contradicted.

**Finding 8 (claim 8): Minimal operational overhead; turnkey acquisition — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:9): "minimal operational overhead. This is a turnkey acquisition opportunity."

Evidence: doc4:17 — 21 days of backup failures. doc4:19 — no backup alerting. doc4:22 — no uptime monitoring. doc3:25 — no CI/CD. doc3:30 — no staging environment. doc4:28 — DNS "Managed personally by 'dave'. No secondary DNS provider." doc4:29 — "No secrets vault" (14 secrets in Heroku config vars).

Gap: The single-dyno managed-service architecture does yield low day-to-day operational complexity, supporting the "minimal overhead" element. However, "turnkey" implies the buyer can take over without remediation. The buyer inherits failing backups with no alerting (doc4:17-19), no monitoring (doc4:22), no CI/CD or staging (doc3:25,30), single-person DNS (doc4:28), and no secrets vault (doc4:29). The overhead is low in operation but the handover requires remediation before it is truly turnkey.

**Finding 9 (claim 9): Standard SaaS agreements; no proprietary lock-in — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:22): "All third-party integrations are on standard SaaS agreements with no proprietary lock-in"; doc9:9: "All third-party integrations are on standard SaaS agreements with no lock-in."

Evidence: doc8:25-28 — "Google OAuth … No contractual relationship. If Google changes API or revokes app, users cannot log in." doc8:29 — GoDaddy DNS "Managed personally by 'dave'. No secondary DNS. If domain expires or GoDaddy has an issue, the app is unreachable." doc8:11-12 — DataEnrich.io: "40% of features depend on this API … Fallback: None implemented … 90 days (either party) termination notice."

Gap: Stripe, Heroku, Redis, and Twilio are standard commercial SaaS services. However, Google OAuth carries no contractual guarantee and is a hard dependency for authentication (doc8:28); DataEnrich.io underpins 40% of features with no fallback and a 90-day exit notice (doc8:11-12); GoDaddy DNS is a single-person-managed single point of failure (doc8:29). The "no lock-in" characterisation understates practical dependency and exit friction.

**Finding 10 (claim 10): Blended MRR $40,000 — [real, minor caveat]**

Claim (doc1:12): "Blended MRR: $40,000"

Evidence: doc5:5 — "Total MRR (Stripe): $16,000." doc5:19 — "3 enterprise companies … have separate contracts for $8,000/mo each, paid via wire transfer." Derived: $16,000 (Stripe) + 3 × $8,000 (wire) = $40,000.

Gap: None in the arithmetic. Minor caveat: 60% of the stated MRR ($24,000 of $40,000) rests on three wire-transfer contracts with defined termination and non-renewal provisions (doc7:10,18,26). Concentration of that magnitude is a revenue-sustainability risk, though the $40k figure itself is supported.

**Finding 11 (claim 11): Asking price $480,000 (12× blended MRR) — [real]**

Claim (doc1:5): "Asking Price: $480,000 (12x blended MRR)"

Evidence: Derived from claim 10 resolution: 12 × $40,000 = $480,000. The stated multiple is arithmetically consistent with the stated MRR.

Gap: None. The arithmetic is correct.

**Finding 12 (claim 12): Mix of high-value enterprise and month-to-month subscribers — [real]**

Claim (doc1:9): "a mix of high-value enterprise contracts and a broad base of month-to-month subscribers."

Evidence: doc5:8-9 — Pro Plan: 91 accounts at $149/mo. doc5:13-14 — Enterprise Plan: 3 accounts in Stripe. doc5:19 — 3 wire-transfer enterprise contracts at $8,000/mo. doc7:29-34 — 94 month-to-month subscriptions with "Auto-renewal" and "No-penalty cancellation."

Gap: None. The two-tier customer mix is confirmed.

**Finding 13 (claim 13): Recurring subscription (monthly and annual enterprise) — [real]**

Claim (doc1:15): "Recurring subscription (Monthly & Annual Enterprise)"

Evidence: doc5:4 — 94 active subscriptions (monthly auto-renew). doc7:5 — Acme "Term: Annual (Renews 2027-03-15)." doc7:14 — GlobalMart "Term: Annual (Renews 2026-11-01)." doc7:22 — ShopStream "Term: Annual (Renews 2027-06-20)."

Claim (doc1:9): "revenue-positive, recurring-revenue SaaS platform"

Evidence: doc5:4 — 94 auto-renewing subscriptions. doc7:31 — "Renewal: Auto-renewal." doc7:5,14,22 — annual enterprise terms. doc5:19 — wire-transfer contracts at $8,000/mo each. Revenue model is subscription-based and recurring.

**Finding 15 (claim 15): Customers range from independent merchants to mid-market enterprise retailers — [real, minor caveat]**

Claim (doc1:9): "ranging from independent merchants to mid-market enterprise retailers."

Evidence: doc5:8-9 — 91 Pro accounts at $149/mo, consistent with independent/small merchants. doc7:5-27 — three enterprise accounts named Acme Retail, GlobalMart, ShopStream, contract values $8,000/mo.

Gap: The breadth of the range (low-$149 to $8k) is supported. The "mid-market enterprise" characterisation of the three named accounts cannot be independently verified from the materials; their size is inferred only from contract value and naming.

**Finding 16 (claim 16): Immediate cash flow — [real]**

Claim (doc1:9): "immediate cash flow"

Evidence: doc5:4-16 — 94 active Stripe subscriptions generating $16,000/mo. doc5:19, doc7:5-27 — three enterprise wire contracts at $8,000/mo each ($24,000/mo). Active billing instruments exist and are generating recurring revenue at the time of the data room.

**Finding 17 (claim 17): Real-time analytics and product intelligence to e-commerce sellers — [real, operational caveat]**

Claim (doc1:9): "real-time analytics and product intelligence to e-commerce sellers"

Evidence: doc8:7-8 — DataEnrich.io provides "product matching, price comparison, category classification." doc8:11 — "40% of features depend on this API." doc8:12 — "If API is down or pricing changes, product degrades to basic mode (no enrichment)."

Gap: The platform does provide analytics and product intelligence as described. Operational caveat: 40% of features are contingent on DataEnrich.io availability with no fallback (doc8:12); a service outage or pricing change degrades the product to a basic mode without enrichment.

**Finding 18 (claim 18): Third-party data-enrichment API supplies real-time product data — [real]**

Claim (doc2:7): "integrate with a third-party data enrichment API that provides real-time product data"

Evidence: doc8:7-8 — "DataEnrich.io … Product data enrichment API (product matching, price comparison, category classification)." doc8:9 — "Cost: $400/mo flat." The API is identified, contracted, and in active use.

**Finding 19 (claim 19): Payment processing via Stripe — [real]**

Claim (doc1:20): "secure payment processing via Stripe"; doc2:6: "Payment processing is securely handled through Stripe."

Evidence: doc5:4 — 94 active Stripe subscriptions. doc8:3-5 — "Stripe … Payment processing. Cost: 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction." doc5:19 — enterprise payments go via wire transfer outside Stripe.

Gap: None. Stripe processes 94 subscriptions at $16k MRR. The claim is accurate for the Stripe-managed payment layer; enterprise wire payments are a separate channel acknowledged in the materials.

**Finding 20 (claim 20): Stripe supports credit-card transactions and recurring billing — [real]**

Claim (doc2:6): "which supports both credit card transactions and recurring billing."

Evidence: doc5:4 — 94 active recurring subscriptions in Stripe. doc8:4 — per-transaction pricing "2.9% + $0.30" confirms credit-card transaction processing. Stripe's recurring-billing capability is confirmed by the active subscription count.

**Finding 21 (claim 21): Rails app hosted on Heroku — [real]**

Claim (doc2:3): "Rails 7 application hosted on Heroku"; doc1:18: "Rails 7 stack."

Claim (doc2:5): "Data persistence is handled by PostgreSQL."

Evidence: doc4:6 — "Database: `heroku-postgresql:standard-0`." This is Heroku's managed PostgreSQL add-on.

**Finding 23 (claim 23): Managed SSL — [real]**

Claim (doc1:20): "Managed SSL"; doc9:12: "automatic SSL."

Evidence: doc4:26 — "SSL: Heroku-managed, auto-renewed."

**Finding 24 (claim 24): Authentication is OAuth — [real]**

Claim (doc1:20): "OAuth authentication."

Evidence: doc8:25-28 — "Google OAuth … Function: Authentication." doc4:29 — "Google OAuth" listed among the 14 Heroku config-var secrets.

**Finding 25 (claim 25): Redis for session caching — [real]**

Claim (doc2:6): "Redis for session caching."

Evidence: doc4:11-13 — "Service: Heroku Redis Add-on. Plan: `heroku-redis:bb-1`. Cost: $50/mo." doc8:17-20 — "Redis (Heroku Add-on) … Function: Caching."

**Finding 26 (claim 26): Deployments, scaling, monitoring streamlined via Heroku dashboard — [partial]**

Claim (doc2:8): "The entire stack is managed through Heroku's dashboard, ensuring that deployments, scaling, and monitoring are streamlined and efficient."

Gap: The Heroku dashboard does provide deployment and dyno-management controls, and the stack is on Heroku. However, "monitoring streamlined and efficient" is contradicted: no uptime monitor is configured (doc4:22). **Finding 27 (claim 27): Stack designed to scale horizontally; one-click dyno addition — [partial]**

Gap: Adding a web dyno via the Heroku dashboard is indeed a one-click action, supporting the literal mechanism claim. However, the architecture is not designed for horizontal scaling: the database shares the single dyno (doc4:6), there are no read replicas (doc4:7), and no separate DB instance exists (doc4:8). **Finding 28 (claim 28): Managed DNS — [real, operational caveat]**

**Finding 30 (claim 30): 30-day retention — [real, operational caveat]**

**Finding 1 (claim 1): "120 active accounts" inflated by 23 phantom records — [partial]**

**Finding 2 (claim 2): "Low churn; stable recurring subscribers" understated by phantom accounts and expiring pilots — [partial]**

**Finding 3 (claim 3): Daily automated backups failing for 21 consecutive days with no alerting — [delta]**

Gap: The claim states that daily automated backups are maintained. The evidence shows the schedule exists but has failed every day for the preceding 21 days with no alerting to flag the outages. The backups are not running. The word "maintain" asserts an ongoing state of operation that the infrastructure config contradicts. At the engagement date (≈2026-08-31, per working record), the most recent successful backup is approximately 32 days old. This is a Tier-1 finding: the recovery point for the entire database is unbounded, and the buyer cannot rely on data integrity or recoverability claims.

**Finding 4 (claim 4): "Platform-level redundancy and automatic failover" — single dyno, single DB, no replicas, no failover target — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:18): "Built on a modern Rails 7 stack with platform-level redundancy and automatic failover." / (doc9:5): "The system has redundancy and automatic failover through Heroku's platform-level process management." / (doc2:3): "automatic scaling and failover capabilities at the platform level."

Gap: The claim describes redundancy and automatic failover. The evidence shows a single web dyno and a single database instance with no read replica, no separate DB, and no standby process. Heroku restarts a crashed dyno, but a restart is recovery of the same single instance, not failover to an independent replica. There is no second compute target and no second database target to fail over to. The architectural description in the claim is contradicted by the configuration.

**Finding 5 (claim 5): "99.9% uptime monitoring" — no uptime monitor of any kind is configured — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:19): "99.9% uptime monitoring and daily automated database backups with 30-day retention." / (doc9:6): "We monitor uptime at 99.9%."

Evidence (doc4:22-23): "Uptime Monitor: None (No Pingdom, UptimeRobot, or custom checks)." (doc4:22). "Status Page: Heroku built-in status page only." (doc4:23).

Lexical search: searched for "uptime," "monitor," "Pingdom," "UptimeRobot," "health check," "status" across all supplied documents. The only uptime-monitor reference is the negative entry at doc4:22. No synthetic check, no external monitor, and no app-level health-check endpoint appear in any supplied document.

Structural search: the infrastructure configuration (doc4) is the expected location for monitoring config. The Monitoring section (doc4:21-23) contains only the negative entry and a pointer to the Heroku platform status page.

Gap: The claim states uptime is monitored at 99.9%. The evidence shows no uptime monitor is configured. The Heroku status page reports Heroku platform health, not the availability of the FlowMetrics application. The claim is contradicted.

**Finding 6 (claim 6): "Automatic scaling; available under varying load without manual intervention" — single dyno, no auto-scale configuration — [delta]**

Claim (doc2:3): "automatic scaling and failover capabilities at the platform level. This ensures that the application remains available even under varying load conditions, with no manual intervention required for routine operations." / (doc1:18): "Scalable Architecture."

Evidence (doc4:5-8): Single `standard-1x` dyno (doc4:5). Single `standard-0` PostgreSQL on the same dyno (doc4:6). No read replicas (doc4:7). No separate DB instance (doc4:8). No auto-scaling, router, scheduler, or performance-dyno configuration appears in any supplied document.

Gap: The claim describes automatic scaling and no-manual-intervention availability under varying load. The evidence shows a single standard dyno with the database sharing the same compute, no read replicas, and no auto-scaling configuration. The stack can restart after a crash (a Heroku platform feature), but the architecture does not scale without manual dyno addition and the database is the single bottleneck. The description overstates the configuration.

**Finding 7 (claim 7): "Comprehensive test coverage across critical paths" — 12 unit tests in utils, zero integration tests, zero payment-path tests — [delta]**

Claim (doc1:21): "Well-documented codebase with comprehensive test coverage across critical paths." / (doc9:7): "The codebase is well-documented with comprehensive test coverage across all critical paths."

Evidence (doc3:26-29): "Unit Tests: 12 (all located in `test/utils/`)" (doc3:27). "Integration Tests: 0" (doc3:28). "Payment-Path Tests: 0" (doc3:29).

Gap: The claim asserts comprehensive coverage across critical paths. The evidence shows 12 unit tests confined to a utils directory, zero integration tests, and zero payment-path tests. The payment path — a critical revenue path for a subscription SaaS — has no test coverage whatsoever. The claim is contradicted.

**Finding 8 (claim 8): "Minimal operational overhead; turnkey acquisition" — no CI/CD, no staging, no monitoring, no backup alerting, single maintainer — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:9): "The business operates with low churn, a scalable technology stack, and minimal operational overhead. This is a turnkey acquisition opportunity."

Gap: The application is currently running on a managed Heroku dyno, so basic platform operations (process restart, SSL renewal) require no daily intervention — that element of the claim holds. However, "minimal operational overhead" and "turnkey" materially understate the remediation a buyer would need to undertake before operating safely: CI/CD, staging, backup alerting, uptime monitoring, DNS redundancy, and single-maintainer knowledge transfer are all absent. **Finding 9 (claim 9): "No proprietary lock-in" — DataEnrich.io carries 40% feature dependency with no fallback — [partial]**

Claim (doc1:22): "All third-party integrations are on standard SaaS agreements with no proprietary lock-in." / (doc9:9): "All third-party integrations are on standard SaaS agreements with no lock-in."

If API is down or pricing changes, product degrades to basic mode (no enrichment)" (doc8:12).

Gap: The contractual agreements are standard SaaS (true), but "no lock-in" understates the functional dependency. 40% of product features depend on a single API with no fallback and a 90-day termination window (doc8:11-12, doc8:10). **Finding 10 (claim 10): "Blended MRR $40,000" — arithmetic checks out, but 60% of revenue is unaudited wire transfers — [real, operational caveat]**

Claim (doc1:9,12): "Our blended Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) stands at $40,000" / "Blended MRR: $40,000"

**Finding 12 (claim 12): "Mix of high-value enterprise and month-to-month subscribers" — confirmed by contract structure — [real]**

Claim (doc1:9): "driven by a mix of high-value enterprise contracts and a broad base of month-to-month subscribers"

Evidence (doc5:8-15; doc7:3-27,29-33): Three enterprise contracts at $8,000/mo each (doc7:6,14,22) and 94 month-to-month Stripe subscriptions (doc7:29-30; doc5:4). The customer base spans a $149/mo Pro plan (91 accounts, doc5:10-11) and $8,000/mo annual enterprise contracts (doc7:3-27).

**Finding 13 (claim 13): "Recurring subscription (Monthly & Annual Enterprise)" — confirmed — [real]**

Claim (doc1:15): "Revenue Model: Recurring subscription (Monthly & Annual Enterprise)"

Evidence (doc5:4): 94 active Stripe subscriptions (doc5:4), which are auto-renewal month-to-month (doc7:30-31). doc7:5,13,21: Three annual enterprise contracts (renewal dates 2027-03-15, 2026-11-01, 2027-06-20). The subscription model is monthly and annual.

Gap: None.

**Finding 14 (claim 14): "Recurring-revenue SaaS platform" — confirmed — [real]**

Claim (doc1:9): "recurring-revenue SaaS platform providing real-time analytics and product intelligence"

Evidence (doc5:4): 94 active Stripe subscriptions confirming recurring revenue. doc2:3: hosted application (SaaS delivery model). doc4:4: hosted on Heroku.
